clue.text: Wearied old dons increased strain?

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the word for increased strain wears the old letter inside it

parts.note: to breed is to increase a stock or strain, so the past tense serves

explanation.surface: Elderly university fellows feeling the pressure mount and getting worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university teachers, but it is the verb meaning puts on, wrapping one piece round the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wearied by tedium is fed up and uninterested, a close synonym.

clue.text: Kosher item appropriate to enthral a dog endlessly?

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the outer word holds the rest inside

parts.note: with the dog in view, the item appropriate is what a dog gnaws
taken as written

indicators.note: the dog's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Fido is the stock name for a pet dog

explanation.surface: Asking whether a gift fit for a dog is properly kosher.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin for 'in good faith'; Fido is the traditional name for a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Kosher is informal for genuine or legitimate, which is what the Latin phrase means.

clue.text: Old woman strapped in checks stays

indicators.note: the old woman is buckled inside the word for checks

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
mother, informally, as in one's old woman

explanation.surface: An elderly lady buckled into corsets and checked clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stays' suggests corsets, but it is the verb meaning continues to be.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain somewhere is to stay there, so the verb forms are synonyms.

clue.text: I'd say fists flying fail to hit the mark

indicators.note: fists flying are thrown about wildly, so the letters scatter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A brawler admits that a flurry of punches missed the target.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissatisfy is to fall short of what someone wanted, a figurative failure to hit the mark.

clue.text: At home, place for batter and mushroom

parts.note: in cricket the batter stands at the crease

explanation.surface: A kitchen scene: batter and a mushroom prepared at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' suggests cooking, but it is the cricketer, whose stand is the crease, a line marked on the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Mushroom as a verb means grow rapidly, a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Tunnels are designed to accommodate task in computer architecture

indicators.note: the rearranged letters house the task inside them
the letters are designed, i.e. laid out anew in another order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange
a task is a piece of work

explanation.surface: Engineers lay out tunnels to fit a particular job.
explanation.definitionFit: These are computing systems modelled on the brain, a kind of machine-learning architecture.

clue.text: Red-eye grounded — it's gone missing here and there!

indicators.note: missing here and there means the letters of gone are lost at scattered places in grounded

explanation.surface: A night flight is grounded, and the plane has vanished from the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red-eye' suggests an overnight flight, which fits 'grounded'; it is a fish. Remove G, O, N and E, one by one, from GROUNDED.
explanation.definitionFit: The rudd is a European freshwater fish with red fins, also known as the red-eye.

clue.text: Roman commander an old man retaining control

indicators.note: the outer letters keep the control word held within them

parts.note: the indefinite article reduced to its single letter
pa is father, one's old man
to have a grip on something is to have control of it

explanation.surface: A Roman general depicted as an elderly man keeping hold of power.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Agrippa was Augustus's leading general, victor at Actium.

clue.text: Tree beginning to exfoliate and lean

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: taken as written; its first letter is used
lean and bony both describe a thin body

explanation.surface: A tree starting to shed its bark and tilting over.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebony is a tropical hardwood tree prized for its black timber.

clue.text: Places for training curates as souls lost

indicators.note: souls that are lost go astray, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Seminaries where clergy are trained, depicted as lost souls.
explanation.definitionFit: Military obstacle tracks used to build soldiers' fitness are where they train.

clue.text: Tyneside dining room seating one's arch-rival?

parts.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England

indicators.note: the dining room seats one, holding it inside

parts.note: a mess is where service personnel eat
one is I; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A Geordie's archenemy sits at their table in the mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside, around Newcastle, gives NE for North East.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a long-standing enemy who keeps defeating one, so a fierce opponent.

clue.text: Open about amount of work experience

indicators.note: the word for open goes around the unit

parts.note: to undo a knot or parcel is to open it
the erg is a physics unit of work

explanation.surface: Talk of being frank about a heavy workload.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo something is to go through it, i.e. to experience it.

clue.text: City in Asia backs political party, overcome with rage

indicators.note: the outer word covers the reversed continent and party

parts.note: the latest rage is a fad

indicators.note: the continent's name runs back to front

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round
Lab is short for Labour

explanation.surface: A city in Asia supporting a party, though gripped by anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Faisalabad is a major industrial city in Punjab, Pakistan.

clue.text: Agile informer at last taken in by mole

indicators.note: the letter is held inside the spy word

parts.note: a mole is a spy planted in an organisation

indicators.note: only the final letter of informer is used

parts.note: taken as written; its last letter is used

explanation.surface: An informer finally caught by a double agent, nimble as he is.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry means lively and nimble, especially of an older person.

clue.text: Work goes into newly arranged musical entertainment

indicators.note: the work goes inside the rearranged letters
newly signals that arranged is to be rearranged afresh

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange
op. is the abbreviation for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A piece of work slotted into a freshly arranged musical show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' seems to describe the music but is the fodder itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand opera is a large-scale sung drama, a form of musical entertainment.

clue.text: Martinet brings nothing round in aspirin dissolved with acid

indicators.note: the reversed nothing goes inside the jumble
an aspirin dissolved in water breaks up, so the letters break up too

parts.note: taken as written as part of the letters to rearrange
taken as written as part of the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: turned round, the word for nothing reads backwards

parts.note: nil means nothing, as in a score

explanation.surface: A strict boss offers nothing except an aspirin fizzing in acid.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a strict enforcer of rules, the same as a stern disciplinarian.

clue.text: Maybe butter in hospital leaving taste less refined

indicators.note: the hospital letter departs from the taste word

parts.note: a hint is a small taste or trace
ruder means coarser, less polished

explanation.surface: Butter in hospital food with less polished flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is not the spread but one who butts in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who butts in, an interloper, is an intruder; 'maybe' marks it as an example.

clue.text: Water feature having unexpected use for instance

indicators.note: an unexpected use rearranges things, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A garden fountain put to some surprising purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water feature' suggests a fountain, but it is a physical property of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Surface tension is the property that lets water form a skin and drops, a characteristic of the liquid.

clue.text: One French girl covering kilometres without a break

parts.note: un is French for one

indicators.note: the girl's name wraps around the kilometre letter

parts.note: Lucy is a girl's name
K is the usual short form for kilometres

explanation.surface: A French girl running kilometres without a pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without a break' suggests nonstop, but it means lacking a lucky break.
explanation.definitionFit: A break is a stroke of luck, so being without one is being unfortunate.

clue.text: Such investigations as bathyscaphe might make?

definitions.meaning: the straight sense: thorough, detailed inquiries
a bathyscaphe is a deep-sea submersible, so its explorations happen far below the surface

explanation.walkthrough: A bathyscaphe is a deep-diving submersible, so its work literally takes place at great depth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorough studies are described as going deep, a common idiom for detailed analysis.

clue.text: None too bright having drink after parking

indicators.note: the drink comes after the parking letter

parts.note: ale is beer

explanation.surface: Someone a bit dim who's had a drink after parking the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'None too bright' suggests stupid, but here it describes a faint colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale colour lacks intensity, so it is not very bright.

clue.text: Jury members mercilessly find fault with Picasso's article?

parts.note: critics pan a show when they slate it
Picasso was Spanish, and el is the Spanish definite article

explanation.surface: Jurors savaging a piece written about Picasso.
explanation.definitionFit: A jury is a panel of people chosen to judge a case.

clue.text: Discharged from brotherhood for misbehaving?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: expelled from a religious order, put out of the order

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the first sense: a monk thrown out of his order.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means unacceptable or improper behaviour, and literally removed from a fraternity.

clue.text: Buzz from live lines

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
L is a line, doubled for lines

explanation.surface: Excitement coming off live telephone lines.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a buzz is British slang for phoning them, as is giving them a bell.

clue.text: Our setter flipping about labyrinthine clue's central part

indicators.note: the reversed word goes around the jumbled clue
the setter word flips round to read backwards

parts.note: the sun is what sets each evening, playing on the crossword setter

indicators.note: a labyrinth is a maze, so the clue letters are twisted around

parts.note: the word clue, with 's read as 'is'

explanation.surface: The setter cursing at the heart of a mazelike clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our setter' looks like the crossword compiler but is the sun, which sets.
explanation.definitionFit: A nucleus is the core or centre of something, such as an atom or cell.

clue.text: This preserves joint record held in work at bakery?

indicators.note: the record sits inside the bakery verb

parts.note: bakers knead dough
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A bakery worker keeps a record of the joint of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' sounds like a cut of meat but is the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A kneepad is protective padding worn to protect the knee joint.

clue.text: Stalwart Cavalier changing sides at the outset

indicators.note: the first letter, right, is switched to its opposite side, left

parts.note: the Cavaliers were royalists in the English Civil War

explanation.surface: A firm supporter of the king switches allegiance from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L stand for right and left, so the opening right becomes left.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalwart is a faithful supporter, the same as a loyalist.

clue.text: Soldiers after injurious charge can't stand

indicators.note: the soldiers come after the charge

parts.note: ABH, actual bodily harm, is a British criminal charge
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Troops facing an assault charge cannot bear it.
explanation.walkthrough: ABH, actual bodily harm, is a UK assault charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to detest it, unable to tolerate it.
